ON A `--shared` GRAPH, `export_graph` WRITES EVERY ATTACHED SEAT'S IN-FLIGHT WORK INTO THE CALLER'S FILE AND REPORTS NOTHING ABOUT IT. Measured repeatedly: 28 foreign nodes in one export, 17 in the next, both landing in the caller's git commit under a message naming none of them; separately a seat declared 67 added of which 30 were not theirs, and a third pre-announced its own carry before it landed. THE SECOND-ORDER EFFECT IS WORSE THAN THE FIRST: the seat whose work was carried then exports and gets a NO-OP against an identical content hash, which reads to them as a failed save. Filed five times across three dates by three seats from three directions — receiving, writing, and pre-emptively — and the recurrence is itself the finding. `sync_status` answers the opposite direction well and explicitly declines this one ('BEING AHEAD OF THE RECORD IS NOT REPORTED'), which is right for a single-writer seat and wrong once 'ahead' can contain work that is not yours. The only reliable discriminator today is diffing the export against HEAD BY NODE ID, a discipline three sessions had to invent separately. FIX SHAPE: `export_graph` already computes what it is about to write and every node is seat-stamped — return a delta naming how many nodes and edges the file gains and which contributors or epochs they carry, plus an explicit `unchanged: true` so 'wrote nothing' and 'wrote something' stop being the same reply. A `dry_run` would be better still. THE ASK IS NOT THAT THE EXPORT REFUSE — only that it stop being silent. || SOURCE: Observed by the dev_storyflow fleet on 2026-08-15, on reflow2 0.31.0 with served == installed verified through /proc/<pid>/exe. Three agent seats, one shared graph, one day.

▸ VERIFIED BY EXPERIMENT 2026-08-15, against the running 0.31.0 build — two seats attached to one `--shared` server, one export file. TWO CLAIMS HOLD AND ONE DOES NOT, and the one that does not hides a sharper defect than the one reported. 
(a) HOLDS. Seat A states a requirement and does not publish it; seat B exports; A's node IS in B's file. Confirmed directly by reading the written document, not inferred. 
(b) HOLDS. The reply carries exactly `bytes, content_hash, edges, nodes, path, prev_content_hash, stamp` — no attribution of any kind, so a caller cannot tell whose work it just published without diffing the file themselves. 
(c) DOES NOT HOLD AS REPORTED. The report says the victim's own export then returns 'a content_hash DIFFERING from prev_content_hash'. It does not. On an export that changes nothing, `prev_content_hash` comes back NULL. 

⭐ BUT THE REAL DEFECT IS UNDERNEATH IT, AND IT IS THE SAME SHAPE AS THE WHO-EDGE ONE: `prev_content_hash: null` MEANS TWO DIFFERENT THINGS AND SAYS NEITHER. Measured: a FIRST-EVER export returns null, and an export that WROTE NOTHING NEW returns null. Same reply, opposite facts — 'I have started the chain' and 'somebody already published my work, so I added nothing'. That second reading is exactly what the reporter experienced and mis-described. 

FIX SHAPE, REVISED BY THE MEASUREMENT and now in two independent parts: (1) DISAMBIGUATE THE NULL — an explicit flag distinguishing first-export from wrote-nothing. Small, self-contained, and it is `dec:three-party-checks` and the `revision` block's principle applied to a third surface. (2) SAY WHOSE WORK IT IS — the delta the reporter asked for: how many nodes and edges the file gains and which contributors or epochs they carry. Larger, needs attribution the export does not currently compute, and it is the half that addresses the ORIGINAL harm of a commit carrying work under a message naming none of it. 

NOTE ONE THING THE EXPERIMENT FOUND BY ACCIDENT: the near-match guard on `add_requirement` fired ACROSS SEATS — seat B was refused because seat A's unpublished node was close in wording. So one cross-seat channel already exists, incidentally, in the one place nobody designed it as such.

▸▸ CORRECTING MY OWN VERIFICATION, MINUTES LATER. THE ▸ NOTE ABOVE IS WRONG ABOUT (c) AND THE ORIGINAL REPORT WAS RIGHT. I wrote that (c) 'does not hold' because a no-op export returned `prev_content_hash: null`. That was an ARTIFACT OF A TWO-STEP TEST: `chain_after` gives an unchanged export the PREDECESSOR'S OWN prev, which was null only because the predecessor was itself the first-ever export. On a chain of any real length it is a hash. Re-measured across five exports: 
    1. first ever          content=9552429a  prev=None
    2. changed             content=f617f1ee  prev=9552429a
    3. UNCHANGED           content=f617f1ee  prev=9552429a   <- byte-identical to row 2
    4. changed again       content=6bf44741  prev=f617f1ee
    5. UNCHANGED again     content=6bf44741  prev=f617f1ee   <- byte-identical to row 4
⇒ AN EXPORT THAT WROTE A CHANGE AND AN EXPORT THAT WROTE NOTHING RETURN THE SAME REPLY, exactly as reported. `content_hash != prev_content_hash` in BOTH cases, so that difference discriminates nothing. The null-vs-hash story in the note above applies only to the first two exports of a file's life and is not the defect. 

THE LESSON, and it is the same one this file keeps producing in a new place: my probe was too short to be representative, and a too-short probe produced a confident refutation of a true report. Three reports checked today, three where the OBSERVATION held; the two consequences I doubted, one was genuinely overstated (the checksum item) and one — this — I refuted wrongly by measuring an unrepresentative case. A verification is evidence about the case you actually ran.

▸ HALF ADDRESSED 2026-08-15 (epoch:an-export-says-whether-it-changed-anything). `export_graph` now returns `wrote: created|changed|unchanged`, plus a note on the `unchanged` case saying what it usually means on a shared server. That closes the part a caller cannot otherwise compute — a no-op and a save were byte-identical replies. VALID_TO IS NOT SET: the ORIGINAL harm is untouched. The export still does not say WHOSE work it is about to publish, so a commit can still carry another seat's nodes under a message naming none of them. That half needs a decision about what attribution means on an export — per contributor, per epoch, or per seat — and is a design question rather than a bug fix.
